description: A 2.78-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 running inference on a single CPU in 8.24 GB of RAM. Portable C99: no BLAS, no framework, no GPU.

latest_release.name: v1.1.0
latest_release.body:
Chat, native Windows builds, an 8 GB class mode for the complete model, NEON kernels for ARM, and a round of hardening on everything that parses checkpoint files. Output is unchanged wherever it was already defined: every oracle gate still matches the PyTorch reference exactly.

**One compatibility note:** `--save-state` files are now version 2, with a checksum. A version 1 file is refused rather than read; regenerate it with `--gen 0 --incremental --save-state`.

## New

- `--chat`: the official K3 XTML chat format, with JSONL history, `--no-think`, `--thinking-effort`, and opt-in sampling through `--temperature`, `--top-p`, `--top-k` and `--seed`. Greedy by default. Later turns reuse the previous turn's state instead of re-prefilling the transcript, behind a bit-exact gate.
- `--preset ultra`: the complete 93-layer model in an 8 GB class memory budget, verified with four full runs on a Jetson Orin Nano Super.
- Native Windows builds through MSYS2 MinGW-w64, with every gate passing, and NEON kernels on arm64.
- Ctrl-C stops at a safe point, still writes the state file, the results and the reports, and exits 5. A second Ctrl-C kills.
- `--stop-id`, `--gen 0` to warm a prefix once and resume it many times, `--threads`, and `--trunk-ring`.
- `download-model.sh <dest> --layers N` fetches only the shards a layer prefix needs, about 7 GB for `N=1`, for trying the pipeline on a disk too small for the checkpoint.

## Faster, output unchanged

- The MXFP4 expert matmul is about 1.6x faster, with another 1.56x from a flat-row AVX2 path.
- Trunk layers are read in parallel chunks and pinned largest-first; expert reads are split into 1 MiB chunks.
- On Linux the thread count now defaults to physical cores, which measured about 1.3x faster per token on a 16-core SMT machine.

## Fixed

- `--preset auto` could not start on machines with roughly 100 GB or more available, and printed a negative shortfall.
- macOS: reads of 2 GiB or more failed, and available memory read as 0, which switched off both memory checks.
- Hardening across the safetensors reader, trunk.json and the JSON parser: integer overflow, out-of-bounds reads, overlapping or gapped tensor spans, and truncated documents. Checked against the released checkpoint's own files, including all 96 shard headers.
- A batched prefill path summed uninitialized memory when an expert failed to load.
- A partial download now names the missing file, using the checkpoint's real file names.
- State files are checksummed and saved by atomic rename, so a failed save no longer destroys the previous one.

## Verification

`make test`, ctest, both sanitizer jobs and the strict-warnings build are green on Linux, macOS and Windows, and every oracle gate matches the PyTorch reference exactly.

Thanks to everyone whose work is in this release: @Avicennasis, @FermiHart, @cablepull, @Deobot2, @BlakeEvans22, @santhoshsathish94, @Irfanwani, @AuricTW, @arafatsolok, @genesisrevelationinc-debug, @TROY665, @openchat-ai, @ysgao, @ShaalanMarwan, @cwwjacobs, @biokraft and @Barba2k2.

Full log in [CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c/blob/v1.1.0/CHANGELOG.md). Diff: [v1.0.0...v1.1.0](https://github.com/FareedKhan-dev/kimi-k3-in-c/compare/v1.0.0...v1.1.0).

detail.readme_excerpt:
kimi-k3-in-c

A 2.78-trillion-parameter model. One CPU. 8 GB of RAM.

Kimi K3 inference in portable C99.
No BLAS. No framework. No GPU.

2.78T
parameters		 1.56 TB
checkpoint on disk		 8.24 GB
peak RSS, measured		 176 KB
the whole engine		 0
GPUs

The same 2.78-trillion-parameter model, the same answer, on whatever machine you own.
More memory only buys speed:

the machine you have RAM time per token what is going on
an ordinary laptop 8 GB 26.5 s the whole model streams off the disk on every step
a high-end laptop 32 GB 24.2 s some of the model now sits in memory
a desktop 64 GB 19.8 s more of it sits in memory
a heavy workstation 128 GB+ 5.6 s the model fits entirely in memory, the disk wait is gone
Same short prompt at every size, and the output is byte-identical from the smallest machine to the largest; only the clock changes. One machine, 124 cores, fast NVMe drive: the first three rows still read the model from disk each step, so a slower drive is slower there, while the 128 GB+ row keeps everything in memory and no longer waits on the disk. On that same machine v1.0.0 made the math per token about 8× lighter, a follow-up question in a chat 3.9× faster, and long prompts about half as costly. (A token is roughly a short word-piece; the two runnable demos below are the original captures on a slower drive, so their clock reads a little higher.) Full data i
